items.title: Asking AI to disagree with you may improve your work
items.content_html:
Instead of asking AI to do your work, consider asking it to challenge your work.

Evidence suggests that heavy reliance on generative AI can reduce critical thinking and erode job skills. The problem of “cognitive offloading”—being too quick to outsource our mental workload to AI—can also lead to shoddy, subpar work.

But knowledge workers who use AI correctly can still gain a significant edge, writes University of Massachusetts (Amherst) Professor Monideepa Tarafdar in The Conversation. The key is to create “friction” by having AI challenge your ideas.

Researching opposing viewpoints has always been a good idea, but it matters even more today because AI models tailor their output based on users’ previous prompts and responses. This tendency can create an “echo chamber” effect that leads the models, and their users, to overlook information that doesn’t fit an established pattern.

To mitigate this vulnerability, Tarafdar says users should ask AI directly for opposing perspectives. For example, a marketing professional in her study asked AI to create virtual customers who disliked the product that the professional was marketing. The AI model’s negative feedback included new ideas for the product that its designers had not considered.

Another research subject, an attorney, asked an AI model to find obscure legal loopholes and game out how they might be exploited, which prompted it to provide “surprising but realistic” scenarios of unethical worker behavior.

Along with her own work, Tarafdar cites outside studies supporting the idea that creating “friction” with AI can improve its performance.

In a study on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations, researchers found that human-AI collaboration produced better results than human-only or AI-only work, and that collaboration involving disagreement produced the best results.

Another study showed that creative writers produce better work when they use AI interactively as a sounding board, rather than to ghostwrite copy on its own.

Tarafdar says leaders should instruct their employees to use “friction-generating queries,” including by drawing on their own knowledge and experience to make the AI question its outputs.

“In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you,” she writes.

items.title: This $100 iPad is the best way to beat the RAM pricing surge
items.content_html:
Macworld

Aple iPad 8th Generation

View Deal

These days, finding an affordable iPad is darn near impossible. If you want to get one for your kids, then spending a ton of money is definitely not on your to-do list since it’s likely to get dropped or damaged. Well, we’ve found a solution: This Apple iPad 8th Gen is only $110 at Woot but if you use code APPLETEN, it’ll take off another 10 percent, bringing it under $100. It’s not new (Woot says it’s in Grade A Refurbished condition) and won’t get the latest features, but it’s about a third of how much you’d pay for a new iPad today.

The 10.2-inch Retina display is sharp and bright enough for movies, e-books, and homework apps. Inside, the A12 Bionic chip with Neural Engine was a big upgrade for this model. When it came out, it made the 8th-gen iPad much faster than the version before it, and it still handles games, streaming, and everyday apps without much fuss. Back in 2020, we called it “the best affordable tablet you can buy,” and that’s definitely the case right now. The tablet won’t support iOS 27 or Apple Intelligence, but you’re getting a perfect device you don’t have to worry about when you hand it over.

Think about it: Sooner or later, every parent hits the same moment on a long car ride or a rainy Saturday: the kids want your phone, and you’d really like it back. A tablet of their own solves that, but handing a pricey new iPad to a seven-year-old is a gamble most of us would rather skip. Well, at $110, you won’t wince every time your kid “gently” puts it on the table. Because it’s refurbished, you’re also giving a perfectly good device a second life instead of buying new, and a landfill somewhere will thank you. It’s guaranteed to be free of major dents and dings, plus it comes with a 90-day warranty in cases there’s anything wrong with it.

For under $100, this older iPad model is an easy pick if you want a kid-friendly first tablet or a simple spare iPad for the house without paying full price.

items.title: One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta
items.content_html:
In a region of Nigeria blighted by decades of pollution, Martha Agbani and her team are not just replanting trees but regaining ownership of their lost lands and livelihoods

A toxic landscape was familiar to Martha Agbani when she was growing up – the smell of crude oil in the air, rivers running black and trees dying on the banks. In Ogoniland, in Nigeria’s oil-exploited Niger delta, Agbani saw the spills rot away the mangrove forests and destroy the livelihoods of communities around her.

Now, she is training women to plant them back – one fragile green shoot at a time.

Continue reading...
